items.stem: Sound is produced by …
items.answer: vibrating objects
items.markingKey: All sound sources vibrate.

items.stem: Describe how a loudspeaker cone produces a sound wave in air.
items.answer: The cone vibrates back and forth; moving forward it pushes air particles together (compression); moving back it leaves a region of spread-out particles (rarefaction); these travel outwards as a longitudinal wave.
items.markingKey: cone vibrates [1]; compressions and rarefactions formed [1]; travel outward longitudinally [1] [3]

items.stem: Describe the bell-jar experiment and explain what it shows.
items.answer: An electric bell rings inside a glass jar; as air is pumped out the sound becomes fainter although the hammer is still seen vibrating; this shows sound needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum.
items.markingKey: air pumped out, sound fades [1]; bell still seen moving [1]; sound needs a medium [1] [3]

items.stem: A diagram of the sound wave from a vibrating guitar string (sound in air) shows 8 compressions spread over a distance of 2.8 m (from the first to the last compression). Work out the wavelength.
items.markingKey: λ = 2.8/7 = 0.4 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A slinky spring pushed back and forth vibrates at 500 Hz. Calculate the time for one complete vibration and state how many compressions it produces in 2.0 s.
items.answer: 0.002 s; 1000 compressions

items.stem: A tuning fork marked 320 Hz is struck in a laboratory in Santiago. (a) State whether sound is a transverse or longitudinal wave and explain. (b) Explain why the fork can be heard better if its base is pressed against a table.
items.answer: (a) Longitudinal: air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel. (b) The table is made to vibrate too; its large surface moves more air.
items.markingKey: (a) Longitudinal [1]; air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel [1] [2] (b) The table is made to vibrate too [1]; its large surface moves more air [1] [2]

items.stem: Sound waves are …
items.answer: longitudinal
items.markingKey: Air particles vibrate parallel to the direction the wave travels.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the motion of the air particles and the motion of the sound wave.
items.answer: Each particle only oscillates back and forth about a fixed position; the wave (pattern of compressions and rarefactions, and energy) travels through the air.
items.markingKey: particles oscillate about fixed positions [1]; energy/wave pattern moves [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why astronauts on a spacewalk must use radios to talk to each other.
items.answer: Space is a vacuum with no particles to carry sound; radio waves are electromagnetic and need no medium.
items.markingKey: no medium for sound [1]; radio EM waves travel through vacuum [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why astronauts on a spacewalk must use radios to talk to each other. (b) Describe how a loudspeaker cone produces a sound wave in air.
items.answer: (a) Space is a vacuum with no particles to carry sound; radio waves are electromagnetic and need no medium. (b) The cone vibrates back and forth; moving forward it pushes air particles together (compression); moving back it leaves a region of spread-out particles (rarefaction); these travel outwards as a longitudinal wave.
items.markingKey: (a) no medium for sound [1]; radio EM waves travel through vacuum [1] [2] (b) cone vibrates [1]; compressions and rarefactions formed [1]; travel outward longitudinally [1] [3]

items.stem: A diagram of the sound wave from a vibrating guitar string (sound in air) shows 3 compressions spread over a distance of 1.6 m (from the first to the last compression). What is the wavelength?
A diagram of the sound wave from a siren shows 5 compressions spread over a distance of 1.6 m (from the first to the last compression). Work out the wavelength.
items.markingKey: λ = 1.6/4 = 0.4 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A loudspeaker vibrates at 425 Hz. Calculate the time for one complete vibration and state how many compressions it produces in 2.0 s.
items.answer: 0.00235 s; 850 compressions

items.stem: A tuning fork marked 440 Hz is struck in a laboratory in Kathmandu. (a) State whether sound is a transverse or longitudinal wave and explain. (b) Explain why the fork can be heard better if its base is pressed against a table.
items.answer: (a) Longitudinal: air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel. (b) The table is made to vibrate too; its large surface moves more air.
items.markingKey: (a) Longitudinal [1]; air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel [1] [2] (b) The table is made to vibrate too [1]; its large surface moves more air [1] [2]

items.stem: A tuning fork marked 440 Hz is struck in a laboratory in Seoul. (a) Describe how the tuning fork produces sound. (b) State whether sound is a transverse or longitudinal wave and explain. (c) Explain why the sound cannot be heard if the fork is in a vacuum.
items.answer: (a) Its prongs vibrate, pushing and pulling the air to form compressions and rarefactions. (b) Longitudinal: air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel. (c) No particles to transmit the vibrations.
items.markingKey: (a) Its prongs vibrate [1]; pushing and pulling the air to form compressions and rarefactions [1] [2] (b) Longitudinal [1]; air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel [1] [2] (c) No particles to transmit the vibrations [1]

items.stem: What is the approximate speed of sound in air?
items.markingKey: About 340 m/s at room temperature.

items.stem: Explain why sound travels faster in solids than in gases.
items.answer: The particles in solids are much closer together and strongly linked, so vibrations are passed on more quickly.
items.markingKey: particles close/strongly bonded [1]; vibrations passed on faster [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the distance between the two people should be large when measuring the speed of sound by the flash-and-bang method.
items.answer: Over a short distance the time is very small, so reaction time is a large fraction of it; a large distance gives a longer time and a smaller percentage error.
items.markingKey: longer time [1]; reaction time smaller fraction [1] [2]

items.stem: A starting pistol is fired 350 m from a timekeeper who sees the smoke and hears the bang 1.03 s later. Work out the speed of sound.
items.markingKey: v = d/t = 350/1.03 = 340 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A starting pistol is fired 250 m from a timekeeper who sees the smoke and hears the bang 0.76 s later. The times recorded are 0.71, 0.74, 0.71, 0.69 s. (a) Calculate the mean time. (b) Calculate the speed of sound. (c) Suggest why the readings vary and how the method could be improved.
items.answer: (a) 0.712 s (b) 351 m/s (c) reaction time varies; use a larger distance, more repeats, or electronic timing with microphones.
items.markingKey: (a) mean [1] (b) v = 250/0.712 [1] = 351 m/s [1] (c) reaction time / improvement [1]; second improvement [1] [5]

items.stem: Zara uses echoes from a school wall to measure the speed of sound. (a) Describe how to carry out the experiment. (b) Explain why timing many echoes gives a more accurate result.
items.answer: (a) Measure 150 m with a tape; stand 75 m from the wall and clap; clap in rhythm with the echo, timing 20 claps. (b) Reaction-time error is shared over many intervals.
items.markingKey: (a) Measure 150 m with a tape [1]; stand 75 m from the wall and clap, clap in rhythm with the echo, timing 20 claps [1] [2] (b) Reaction-time error is shared over many intervals (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2]

items.stem: In which material does sound travel fastest?
items.answer: Steel
items.markingKey: Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases.

items.stem: Describe how to measure the speed of sound using two microphones and a fast timer.
items.answer: Place two microphones a measured distance apart in line with a sound source; the first starts the timer and the second stops it as the sound passes; v = distance/time.
items.markingKey: two microphones a measured distance apart [1]; timer started/stopped by each [1]; v = d/t [1] [3]

items.stem: Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air and 4000 m/s in wood. Explain this difference in terms of particles, and state in which material a sound would take less time to travel 1 km.
items.answer: Wood: particles are closer together / more strongly linked, so vibrations pass on faster; it takes 0.25 s compared with 2.94 s.
items.markingKey: particle explanation [1]; correct material [1]; times [1] [3]

items.stem: Samuel stands 50 m from a large wall and claps. The echo is heard 0.292 s later. Calculate the speed of sound.
items.markingKey: v = 2d/t = 100/0.292 = 343 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A starting pistol is fired 400 m from a timekeeper who sees the smoke and hears the bang 1.14 s later. Determine the speed of sound.
items.markingKey: v = d/t = 400/1.14 = 351 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: During a storm, Mei counts 8 s between a lightning flash and the thunder. Sound travels at 330 m/s. Calculate the distance to the storm in km and explain why the time for the light can be ignored.
items.answer: 2.64 km; light travels so fast (3 × 10⁸ m/s) that it arrives almost instantly.
items.markingKey: d = vt [1] = 2.64 km [1]; light time negligible [1] [3]

items.stem: Two students stand 400 m apart on a sports field in Toronto The times recorded are 1.19, 1.1, 1.17, 1.11 s. (a) Calculate the mean time. (b) Calculate the speed of sound. (c) Suggest why the readings vary and how the method could be improved.

items.stem: Zara uses echoes from a school wall to measure the speed of sound. (a) The sound travels 100 m to the wall and back in 0.294 s. Calculate the speed of sound. (b) Explain why timing many echoes gives a more accurate result.
items.answer: (a) 340 m/s (b) Reaction-time error is shared over many intervals.
items.markingKey: (a) v = d/t (method/substitution) [1]; answer 340 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) Reaction-time error is shared over many intervals (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2]

items.stem: Ines uses echoes from a school wall to measure the speed of sound. (a) Describe how to carry out the experiment. (b) Explain why timing many echoes gives a more accurate result. (c) State why the wall should be large and flat. (d) Suggest why the value might differ on a cold day.
items.answer: (a) Measure 200 m with a tape; stand 100 m from the wall and clap; clap in rhythm with the echo, timing 20 claps. (b) Reaction-time error is shared over many intervals. (c) To give a clear, strong echo. (d) The speed of sound in air depends on temperature (slower in colder air).

items.stem: The pitch of a sound depends on its …
items.answer: frequency
items.markingKey: Higher frequency → higher pitch.

items.stem: Two oscilloscope traces show sounds A and B. A has twice as many waves on the screen as B, with the same height. Compare the sounds.
items.answer: A has double the frequency so a higher pitch; same amplitude so the same loudness.
items.markingKey: A higher pitch/frequency [1]; same loudness [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a dog can hear a dog whistle but its owner cannot.
items.answer: The whistle’s frequency is above 20 kHz, beyond the upper limit of human hearing, but within a dog’s range.
items.markingKey: above 20 kHz [1]; within dog’s range [1] [2]

items.stem: An oscilloscope is set to 10 ms per division. One complete wave of a sound occupies 8 divisions horizontally. Determine the frequency of the sound.
items.markingKey: T = 10 × 8 = 80 ms; f = 1/T = 12.5 Hz. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An oscilloscope is set to 2 ms per division. One complete wave of a sound occupies 2.5 divisions horizontally. Calculate the frequency and state whether a person with normal hearing could hear it.
items.answer: 200 Hz; yes, it is within 20 Hz–20 kHz.

items.stem: A microphone connected to an oscilloscope shows one full wave every 5 divisions at 5 ms per division. (a) Calculate the frequency. (b) Describe the trace for a higher-pitched sound of the same loudness.
items.answer: (a) 40 Hz (b) Same height, waves closer together.
items.markingKey: (a) correct method/substitution [1]; answer 40 Hz with unit [1] [2] (b) Same height [1]; waves closer together [1] [2]

items.stem: The loudness of a sound depends on its …
items.answer: amplitude
items.markingKey: Larger amplitude → louder.

items.stem: Explain why older people often cannot hear very high-pitched sounds.
items.answer: The upper limit of hearing falls with age (and exposure to loud noise), so high frequencies are no longer detected.
items.markingKey: upper limit decreases with age [1]; high frequencies not detected [1] [2]

items.stem: A guitar string is plucked harder. Explain how the sound changes and how it stays the same.
items.answer: Larger amplitude of vibration so louder; frequency (pitch) depends on the string’s length and tension, so it stays the same.
items.markingKey: louder, larger amplitude [1]; same pitch [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why older people often cannot hear very high-pitched sounds. (b) A guitar string is plucked harder. Explain how the sound changes and how it stays the same.

items.answer: (a) 0.004 s (b) Yes (c) Same spacing, smaller height.

items.stem: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency …
items.answer: above 20 kHz
items.markingKey: Above the upper limit of human hearing.

items.stem: An echo is …
options: a sound absorbed by a wall
a sound that has been amplified
items.answer: a reflected sound wave
items.markingKey: Sound reflects off hard surfaces.

items.stem: Explain how ultrasound is used to detect a crack inside a metal casting.
items.answer: Ultrasound pulses are sent into the metal; some are reflected from the crack and return earlier than those reflected from the far side; the time delay shows the crack’s depth.
items.markingKey: pulses sent in [1]; reflection from crack returns early [1]; time gives depth [1] [3]

items.stem: A bat emits an ultrasound pulse and hears the echo from a moth 0.01 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Calculate the distance to the moth.
items.markingKey: d = vt/2 = 340 × 0.01 ÷ 2 = 1.7 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A fishing boat near Singapore uses sonar. (a) The echo returns after 0.6 s (speed in water 1500 m/s). Calculate the depth. (b) Give one other use of ultrasound.
items.answer: (a) 450 m (b) Prenatal scanning / crack detection / cleaning.

items.stem: Explain why soft furnishings reduce echoes in a hall.

items.stem: Explain why a ship’s sonar uses ultrasound rather than audible sound.

items.answer: (a) Each particle only oscillates back and forth about a fixed position; the wave (pattern of compressions and rarefactions, and energy) travels through the air. items.markingKey: (a) particles oscillate about fixed positions [1]; energy/wave pattern moves [1] [2] (b) cone vibrates [1]; compressions and rarefactions formed [1]; travel outward longitudinally [1] [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the difference between the motion of the air particles and the motion of the sound wave. (b) Explain why astronauts on a spacewalk must use radios to talk to each other.
items.answer: (a) Each particle only oscillates back and forth about a fixed position; the wave (pattern of compressions and rarefactions, and energy) travels through the air. (b) Space is a vacuum with no particles to carry sound; radio waves are electromagnetic and need no medium.
items.markingKey: (a) particles oscillate about fixed positions [1]; energy/wave pattern moves [1] [2] (b) no medium for sound [1]; radio EM waves travel through vacuum [1] [2]

items.stem: A diagram of the sound wave from a tuning fork shows 3 compressions spread over a distance of 1.6 m (from the first to the last compression). Calculate the wavelength.
items.markingKey: λ = 1.6/2 = 0.8 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A vibrating guitar string (sound in air) vibrates at 425 Hz. Calculate the time for one complete vibration and state how many compressions it produces in 2.0 s.
items.answer: 0.00235 s; 850 compressions

items.stem: A tuning fork marked 512 Hz is struck in a laboratory in Cape Town. (a) State whether sound is a transverse or longitudinal wave and explain. (b) Calculate the period of the vibration. (c) Explain why the sound cannot be heard if the fork is in a vacuum. (d) Explain why the fork can be heard better if its base is pressed against a table.
items.answer: (a) Longitudinal: air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel. (b) 0.00195 s (c) No particles to transmit the vibrations. (d) The table is made to vibrate too; its large surface moves more air.
items.markingKey: (a) Longitudinal [1]; air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel [1] [2] (b) T = 1/f: 0.00195 s [1] (c) No particles to transmit the vibrations [1] (d) The table is made to vibrate too [1]; its large surface moves more air [1] [2]

items.stem: The approximate speed of sound in water is …
items.markingKey: About 1500 m/s.

items.stem: Sound travels at about 4000 m/s in wood and 5000 m/s in steel. Explain this difference in terms of particles, and state in which material a sound would take less time to travel 1 km.
items.answer: Steel: particles are closer together / more strongly linked, so vibrations pass on faster; it takes 0.2 s compared with 0.25 s.
items.markingKey: particle explanation [1]; correct material [1]; times [1] [3]

items.stem: A starting pistol is fired 300 m from a timekeeper who sees the smoke and hears the bang 0.87 s later. Calculate the speed of sound.
items.markingKey: v = d/t = 300/0.87 = 345 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A starting pistol is fired 150 m from a timekeeper who sees the smoke and hears the bang 0.43 s later. Determine the speed of sound.
items.markingKey: v = d/t = 150/0.43 = 349 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Sipho uses echoes from a school wall to measure the speed of sound. (a) Describe how to carry out the experiment. (b) The sound travels 100 m to the wall and back in 0.294 s. Calculate the speed of sound.
items.answer: (a) Measure 100 m with a tape; stand 50 m from the wall and clap; clap in rhythm with the echo, timing 20 claps. (b) 340 m/s
items.markingKey: (a) Measure 100 m with a tape [1]; stand 50 m from the wall and clap, clap in rhythm with the echo, timing 20 claps [1] [2] (b) v = d/t (method/substitution) [1]; answer 340 m/s with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Frequency is the number of … (b) State what happens to the pitch of a note if its frequency is doubled.
items.answer: (a) vibrations per second (b) The pitch becomes higher (one octave higher).
items.markingKey: (a) Measured in hertz (Hz). (b) [1]

items.stem: A student studies oscilloscope traces of sounds. The time period is reduced to one third. Predict, with a reason, how the frequency changes.
items.answer: The frequency triples.
items.markingKey: Using f = 1/T: frequency ∝ time period^-1.00; factor = 0.333^-1.00 = 3.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: An oscilloscope is set to 10 ms per division. One complete wave of a sound occupies 2.5 divisions horizontally. Determine the frequency of the sound.
items.answer: 40 Hz
items.markingKey: T = 10 × 2.5 = 25 ms; f = 1/T = 40 Hz. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An oscilloscope is set to 0.5 ms per division. One complete wave of a sound occupies 2.5 divisions horizontally. Calculate the frequency and state whether a person with normal hearing could hear it.
items.answer: 800 Hz; yes, it is within 20 Hz–20 kHz.

items.stem: A microphone connected to an oscilloscope shows one full wave every 2 divisions at 2 ms per division. (a) Calculate the frequency. (b) Describe the trace for a higher-pitched sound of the same loudness.
items.answer: (a) 250 Hz (b) Same height, waves closer together.
items.markingKey: (a) correct method/substitution [1]; answer 250 Hz with unit [1] [2] (b) Same height [1]; waves closer together [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why soft furnishings reduce echoes in a hall. (b) Explain why a ship’s sonar uses ultrasound rather than audible sound.
items.answer: (a) Soft, porous materials absorb sound energy instead of reflecting it, so less sound is reflected back. (b) Ultrasound has a short wavelength, so it forms a narrow beam and gives detailed reflections; it is also not heard by people.
items.markingKey: (a) absorb rather than reflect [1]; weaker echoes [1] [2] (b) narrow beam / detail [1]; inaudible [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why soft furnishings reduce echoes in a hall. (b) Explain how ultrasound is used to detect a crack inside a metal casting.
items.answer: (a) Soft, porous materials absorb sound energy instead of reflecting it, so less sound is reflected back. (b) Ultrasound pulses are sent into the metal; some are reflected from the crack and return earlier than those reflected from the far side; the time delay shows the crack’s depth.
items.markingKey: (a) absorb rather than reflect [1]; weaker echoes [1] [2] (b) pulses sent in [1]; reflection from crack returns early [1]; time gives depth [1] [3]

items.stem: In a medical scan, an ultrasound pulse travels into the body at 1540 m/s and is reflected from an organ boundary, returning after 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ s. Calculate the depth of the boundary below the skin.
items.answer: 4 cm
items.markingKey: d = vt/2 = 1540 × 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 2 = 4 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A fishing boat near Singapore uses sonar. (a) State what is meant by ultrasound. (b) The echo returns after 0.4 s (speed in water 1500 m/s). Calculate the depth. (c) Explain why a pulse, rather than a continuous wave, is used. (d) Give one other use of ultrasound.
items.answer: (a) Sound with frequency above 20 kHz. (b) 300 m (c) So that the time for each reflection can be measured. (d) Prenatal scanning / crack detection / cleaning.
items.markingKey: (a) Sound with frequency above 20 kHz [1] (b) vt/2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 300 m with unit [1] [2] (c) So that the time for each reflection can be measured [1] (d) Prenatal scanning / crack detection / cleaning [1]
